Resolution 25, passed in February 1946, picks the ground: Westchester County in New York, or Fairfield County in Connecticut, close to New York City. A headquarters team must go to the area at once. How states must treat each other was spelled out in full in Resolution 2625, adopted by the General Assembly in 1970. Its annex holds the Declaration on Principles of International Law concerning Friendly Relations and Cooperation among States. A special team had worked on the rules since 1962, meeting last in Geneva in the spring of 1970. Their report lay before the Assembly.

The rules rest on the Charter. States are equal in rights. None may use force against the land or freedom of another. The text is still a base stone of world law.

The pact grew from the Charter's faith in the worth of each human person. The pact sets out the civil, civic, trade, and social rights of each child. States that join it bind themselves in world law to guard those rights. It took force on 2 September 1990. Ratified by more states than any other rights pact in the UN shelf, it is the base text for the rights of children across the world.

dart-australopithecus-africanus-1925:

jaufre-occitan-breuer-1925:

ginza-rba-lidzbarski-1925:

spence-atlantis-in-america-1925:

achad-anatomy-of-the-body-of-god-1925:

yeats-a-vision-1925:

leadbeater-masters-and-the-path-1925:

james-warning-to-the-curious-1925:

shinn-game-of-life-1925:

panchatantra-ryder-1925:

It remains a monument of translation and of the epic it carries.
epictetus-discourses-enchiridion-oldfath:
W A Oldfather published Volume 1 of his Loeb Epictetus in 1925, the standard scholarly English translation. Epictetus was a Greek slave in Rome who won freedom and taught Stoic philosophy. His student Arrian wrote down the Discourses, and Oldfather's first volume holds Books 1 and 2.

Epictetus taught that events lie outside our control, but our judgments about them lie within it. Freedom, he said, is wanting things to happen as they do. The Discourses speak in a direct, searching voice, questioning students by name. Oldfather's Greek text and facing English made the Loeb set the core text of Roman Stoicism for scholars and general readers alike.
mendel-experiments-plant-hybridisation-b:
Gregor Mendel was an Austrian monk who crossed pea plants and counted how their traits passed to the next crop. He read his results to a local science society in 1865, but few people noticed them at the time. William Bateson later translated the paper into English, and this edition came out in 1925.

Mendel found that traits such as tall or short stems appear in clear ratios, not blended halfway. He argued that hidden factors, now called genes, carry each trait from parent to child. The paper was ignored for decades, then rediscovered around 1900. It is now read as the founding work of genetics, the science of heredity.
eliot-hollow-men-1925:
T. S. Eliot published The Hollow Men in 1925, between The Waste Land and his religious poems. The short work runs in five parts, complete here. Its title joins a line from Conrad with the stuffed effigies burned on Guy Fawkes Day in England.

The hollow men are stuffed men, leaning together like scarecrows, unable to act or truly speak. They drift in a dead land between death and any real afterlife, afraid to meet the eyes that judge them. The poem ends with one of the most famous last lines in modern poetry. It captures the spiritual exhaustion of Europe after the First World War.
woolf-mrs-dalloway-1925:
Virginia Woolf published Mrs Dalloway in 1925, after reshaping it from an earlier short story. The whole novel fits inside a single June day in London, just after the First World War. Woolf used what she called a tunnelling method, digging into her characters' pasts as they walk the city.

Clarissa Dalloway buys flowers and prepares an evening party, her mind circling old loves and choices. Across London, the shell-shocked veteran Septimus Smith sinks toward suicide under visions of his dead officer. The two never meet, yet the party scene joins their stories at the close. Woolf's flowing sentences remade the English novel. Mrs Dalloway is now her most widely read book.
glasgow-barren-ground-1925:
Ellen Glasgow considered Barren Ground, published in 1925, her best novel. Glasgow wrote it after years of success with Richmond society stories. This time she set her story on worn-out Virginia farmland and made a working woman its hero.

Dorinda Oakley is betrayed in love as a young woman and flees to New York. She returns home determined to restore her family's ruined farm by science and sheer will. Across thirty years she drains, plants, and prospers, while love offers her a second, harder choice. Glasgow reverses the usual plot: the land, not a husband, is the prize worth winning. Barren Ground is a landmark of American regional fiction.
hemingway-in-our-time-1925:
Ernest Hemingway published In Our Time in New York in 1925, his first book with a major American publisher. Hemingway had built the collection from stories written in Paris, where he worked among the modernist writers of the Left Bank. The book made his reputation.

Nick Adams grows up across the stories: fishing in Michigan, wounded in the war, drifting through Europe after it. Between the tales, short brutal vignettes show bullfighters, soldiers, and refugees. Hemingway's style, short sentences and telling omissions, changed American prose at a stroke. Stories like Big Two-Hearted River and The Doctor and the Doctor's Wife remain classics. In Our Time is the founding book of his career.
anderson-dark-laughter-1925:
Sherwood Anderson published Dark Laughter in 1925, and it became the only bestseller of his career. Anderson had worked in Chicago newspaper rooms and Ohio factories, and both worlds meet here. The novel is also famous sideways: Hemingway's Torrents of Spring parodied its manner to break with Anderson's influence.

Bruce Dudley, a Chicago journalist, walks out on his wife and his job and drifts downriver under a new name. He takes factory work in Indiana and watches his employer's unhappy wife, drawn to the unforced laughter of Black workers around the plant. Anderson sets instinct against a tired, talkative civilization. The writing is loose and incantatory. Dark Laughter is his strangest popular success.
lewis-arrowsmith-1925:
Sinclair Lewis published Arrowsmith in 1925, turning from small-town business to American science. He researched the novel with a young bacteriologist, Paul de Kruif, who supplied the laboratory life. The book was awarded the Pulitzer Prize, which Lewis famously refused.

Martin Arrowsmith fights his way from a prairie town to medical school, country practice, and a great research institute. Everywhere, commerce, publicity, and careerism press him to sell his science short. A plague outbreak in the Caribbean tests his principles at the highest cost. Lewis makes the researcher's purity both heroic and impossible to keep clean. Arrowsmith made the scientist a tragic American hero and remains the classic novel of the profession.
cather-professors-house-1925:
Godfrey St. Peter, a history professor in a lakeside college town, stands at the center of The Professor's House. Willa Cather published the novel in 1925. St. Peter has won fame and money, yet he feels empty in his fine new house and clings to his old study.

Set inside the main story is Tom Outland's tale of a summer in the Southwest. There Tom and a friend find a lost cliff city on a high mesa. Their find brings wonder, then betrayal and loss. Cather joins the two stories to weigh ambition, family duty, and the pull of a purer, vanished world.
proust-guermantes-way-moncrieff-1925:
The Guermantes Way, third volume of In Search of Lost Time, appeared in French in 1920. C. K. Scott Moncrieff's English translation followed in 1925. The narrator, now older, longs to enter the world of the Guermantes, the grand family whose name has charmed him since childhood.

Inside their salons he finds wit, cruelty, and hollow ritual in place of magic. The Dreyfus Affair splits dinner parties and friendships across Paris. His grandmother's decline and death give the volume its grave, tender core. Proust dissects snobbery with a surgeon's patience and a poet's eye. The book shows high society as a theater where everyone performs and few connect.
dictys-dares-trojan-war-latin-1825:
Dictys of Crete and Dares the Phrygian claimed to have fought at Troy and written the war down day by day. Their Latin chronicles, printed together in this 1825 edition, are in fact works of late antiquity. For the medieval West, though, they were the true Troy, read as fact while Homer was hardly known.

Dictys gives a soldier's diary from the Greek camp, and Dares tells the fall of the city from the Trojan side. Both strip out the gods and leave hard war, treachery, and loss. Their plain tales fed the Troy books of the Middle Ages. No public domain English version exists, so the Latin stands as the record.
zorzi-de-harmonia-mundi-1525:
Francesco Zorzi, a Venetian Franciscan, published De Harmonia Mundi Totius, On the Harmony of the Whole World, at Venice in 1525. He dedicated the work to Pope Clement VII. The text is in Latin. Zorzi aimed at nothing less than one system in which Plato, the Kabbalah, music, and Christian faith would sing in tune.

He builds the world on number and proportion, from the music of the spheres to the measures of the temple. Hebrew letters, Greek philosophy, and the gospel expound one another in his pages. The Inquisition later eyed the book with suspicion, which adds to its fame. Zorzi shows the Franciscan mind of the Renaissance at its most daring and most learned.
camden-annales-1625:
William Camden, the antiquary who mapped Britain's past, wrote his Annales on the reign of Queen Elizabeth. The Latin work appeared in parts from 1615, and the English translation of 1625 gives it here as The True and Royall History of Queen Elizabeth. Camden had lived through the reign and knew many of its actors.

Year by year, the Annales record plots, wars, parliaments, and the long defense against Spain. Camden's care for records made his book the first near-official history of the Elizabethan age. Later historians built on his groundwork for centuries. The prose keeps an antiquary's love of fact, names, and dates. It remains a base source for the reign.
descartes-geometry-smith-latham-1925:
Rene Descartes published La Geometrie in 1637 as an appendix to his Discourse on Method. David Eugene Smith and Marcia L. Latham translated it for Open Court in 1925. Their edition adds a facsimile of the first edition beside the English. Descartes united algebra and geometry, two fields long kept apart.

Points become pairs of numbers, and curves become equations. Problems once solved by ruler tricks turn into algebra that any student can run. The method created analytic geometry and changed math teaching for good. Readers also see Descartes setting notation we still use. The book that married algebra to geometry rewards a slow read.
principia-mathematica-vol-1-1925:
Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell sought to ground all mathematics in logic in Principia Mathematica. Volume one appeared first in 1910, and the text here is the second edition of 1925. Russell wrote a new introduction for that edition. The volume runs through the sections numbered from star one to star forty-three.

Inside, the authors build numbers and classes from pure logical notions. Their dense symbols fill page after page of careful proof. Even simple truths take long chains of steps to secure. The project, called logicism, set the terms for later work on foundations. Few books match its ambition or its rigor. Volume one opens a three volume set.
spr-proceedings-vol35-1925:
Parts ninety three through ninety six make volume thirty five, printed in 1925. The Society for Psychical Research nears the end of the span its archive is known for. Telepathy trials take their place beside reports of sittings and cases. Mediums old and new face the society's practiced tests.

Records of sittings run long, with sitters testing claims against private facts. Apparition reports continue under the old standards of proof. Skeptics within the society publish beside the convinced. Volume thirty five keeps the journal of record true to its founding bargain. Evidence and doubt share the binding. The long debate of the era breathes in these pages.
stendhal-charterhouse-parma-moncrieff-19:
Fabrice del Dongo rides into Waterloo half understanding what he sees, in Stendhal's Charterhouse of Parma. C. K. Scott Moncrieff's 1925 translation, complete in two volumes, carries Balzac's praised masterpiece of court life at Parma. Balzac himself called it among the century's greatest novels, and his study of Stendhal rides along in this edition.

Prison, a great-aunt's schemes, and a forbidden love shape Fabrice's path through a petty, sparkling court. Stendhal writes fast and dry, letting politics and passion share every scene. The charterhouse of the title waits at the end as refuge, the quiet close of a life spent chasing joy.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol25:
Volume XXV of the Journal of Discourses, from Liverpool in 1885, stands second from last in the set. Shorthand reports preserve sermons by the church's senior men, preached in a season of raids and trials over marriage law. The pulpit voice here is by turns defiant, patient, and pastoral.

Thirty years of the Journal had made it the movement's great storehouse of spoken teaching. This volume adds the words of leaders who knew the founding age at first hand. Readers who follow the set to its end meet, in Volume XXV, the old church at its most embattled.
woolf-common-reader-1925:
Virginia Woolf published The Common Reader in 1925, gathering essays she had written for journals over the previous decade. The title states her creed: these pieces address the ordinary reader who reads for pleasure, not the scholar.

Essays take up Jane Austen, the modern novel, the Elizabethans, and the art of reading itself. 'Modern Fiction' argues that the novel must catch life as it falls on the mind, not as plots arrange it. Woolf's voice is light, exact, and quietly radical. The collection defined a new way of writing about books, intimate and free, and it is still a model of the essay.
lawrence-st-mawr-1925:
St. Mawr, published in 1925, is a novella of Lou Witt, a rich American woman in England. Her husband seems hollow to her, and her social world seems dead. At a country sale she buys St. Mawr, a magnificent stallion, and the horse changes everything.

The stallion stands for a wild, male vitality that modern England has lost, and Lou follows that force rather than the men around her. She ends at a ranch in New Mexico, choosing the desert and the horse's world over marriage. The tale is Lawrence's flight motif at its purest, and many call it his finest novella.
ford-no-more-parades-1925:
No More Parades, published in 1925, is the second volume of Parade's End and its great war book. Christopher Tietjens now serves as an officer in France, holding a draft of men together under shelling, mud, and absurd orders.

Sylvia follows him to the front, trailing scandal, while his mind keeps returning to Valentine Wannop and the England that is vanishing. Ford, who served himself, writes battle as confusion, noise, and moral pressure rather than glory. The trenches are rendered as a modernist time-piece, memory and terror interleaved. Many judge this the finest volume of the four.
stein-making-of-americans-1925:
The Making of Americans, published in 1925, is Stein's thousand-page novel of everyone. Begun as a history of one family, the Herslands, it swells into an attempt to describe every kind of person who has ever lived.

Stein's prose circles and repeats, working out her idea that character shows itself in the bottom nature of each person, endlessly restated. Whole chapters turn on tiny variations of a single sentence. Few readers finish it; many writers have been changed by trying. It is the long laboratory of her continuous present, the experiment behind all her later work.
williams-american-grain-1925:
William Carlos Williams, a New Jersey doctor and poet, wrote In the American Grain in 1925 as a counter-history of America. Against the smooth schoolbook story, he sets raw encounters between the Old World and the New.

Chapters take up Columbus, Cotton Mather, Daniel Boone, and Poe, each rendered in a prose that shifts voice to match its subject. Williams hunts for a usable past: the local, earthy contact he thought American writing needed. The book argues that America's true grain lies in its ground and its speech. It became a sourcebook for poets seeking an American idiom.
kafka-der-prozess-1925:
Der Prozess, The Trial, appeared in 1925, a year after Kafka's death, published by the Verlag Die Schmiede against his instruction to burn his papers. Josef K., a bank official, is arrested one morning for a crime that is never named.

K. fights through a court that sits in attics, works by rumor, and never states its charge. Lawyers, painters, and priests offer help that helps nothing. The novel ends with an execution 'like a dog'. In the original German, its bureaucratic nightmare reads at full chill. It is the defining novel of guilt without cause.
russell-abc-relativity-1925:
The ABC of Relativity, published in 1925, is Russell's popular account of Einstein's special and general relativity. Einstein had remade physics, and the public needed a guide who could write clearly. Russell, a philosopher of mathematics, took the task.

He explains why events called simultaneous may not be, how gravity becomes geometry, and what the famous tests showed, using trains, lifts, and clocks instead of equations. The book avoids false simplicity: Russell admits where the ideas strain common sense and says why they must be accepted anyway. It became the standard lay introduction of its era and still serves readers well.
santayana-dialogues-limbo-1925:
Dialogues in Limbo, published in 1925, sets Santayana's arguments among the dead, in the Platonic manner. In limbo, shades of Alcibiades, Democritus, Dionysius, and a modern stranger debate philosophy, religion, and the modern world without the heat of the living.

Santayana speaks largely through the Stranger, testing his views on nature against ancient thought and modern faith. The dialogue form lets doubts be voiced that a treatise would suppress. Death gives the speakers leisure and honesty in equal measure. The book is playful, serene, and quietly radical, a favorite among his readers for its ease of manner.
broad-mind-place-nature-1925:
The Mind and Its Place in Nature, published in 1925 from Broad's Tarner Lectures, is his classic work on the philosophy of mind. He surveys seventeen possible theories of how mind and body relate, and eliminates them one by one.

Mechanism and vitalism are both weighed and found partial; Broad defends an emergent view, in which mind arises from the body without being reducible to it. He also gives psychical research a fair hearing, having studied it for years. The book's patience and range are legendary. It remains a model of how to think through a hard problem in public.
collingwood-outlines-philosophy-art-1925:
Outlines of a Philosophy of Art, published in 1925, is Collingwood's early book on aesthetics. It is a sketch toward the theory he would complete years later in The Principles of Art. Its central claim is already his: art is imaginative expression.

Collingwood sets art apart from craft, amusement, and magic by one test. The artist does not know what he feels until he has expressed it. Making is discovery, not manufacture to a plan. The book is short, brisk, and argumentative. It lets readers watch a major theory of art in its first, clear form.
trotsky-literature-revolution-1925:
Literature and Revolution, published in English in 1925 in Rose Strunsky's translation, is Leon Trotsky's theory of art after the Russian Revolution. The exiled revolutionary, then still a leader of the Soviet state, surveys Russian literature and asks what culture the new order should want.

Trotsky defends artistic freedom against party bureaucrats, arguing that art must work by its own laws, while he judges writers by their stance toward the revolution. Futurists, formalists, and fellow travelers are weighed with wit and severity. The book is a paradox: a Marxist classic against socialist realism. Its intelligence survives its moment.
laski-grammar-politics-1925:
A Grammar of Politics, published in 1925, is Laski's systematic political theory. It is the fullest statement of his pluralist thought and his democratic socialism. The state, liberty, equality, rights, and property are treated in turn, in the manner of a grammar: the elements and rules of the subject.

Laski argues that rights are conditions of social welfare. Liberty, he says, needs economic equality to be real, and government must be judged by the lives it makes possible. The book is dense with learning and warm with reforming purpose. It became the standard text of the British left between the wars.
locke-new-negro-1925:
The New Negro, published in 1925 and edited by Alain Locke, is the landmark anthology of the Harlem Renaissance. Locke, a Howard philosopher, gathered the movement's fiction, poetry, essays, and art. His aim was to present a people remade in its own image.

His title essay declares that the Negro is no longer an object of history but a maker of it. The people, he argues, are moving from the rural South to the modern city. Work from the era's rising writers and artists fills the volume with argument and display. The book served as the movement's manifesto and showcase in one. Its influence on American culture is still unfolding.
plos-pone-0003425:
Liran I. Shlush and co-authors checked a claimed longevity marker in this 2008 study. Studies in northern Italy and Finland tied one mitochondrial DNA group to long life. That group, haplogroup J, appeared more often among people past one hundred. The team tested the claim in Ashkenazi Jewish centenarians.

Their long-lived group showed no extra share of haplogroup J. The marker's link to long life did not hold in this population. Negative results like this keep longevity genetics honest. A marker found in one group may mean little in another. Long life likely rests on many small factors rather than one marker.
plos-pone-0003525:
Boris Schmid, Can Keşmir, and Rob J. de Boer modeled HIV escape and human diversity in this 2008 paper. MHC class I molecules vary greatly between people. That variety lowers the chance a virus arrives pre-adapted to a new host. Still, HIV might dodge shared steps of antigen processing instead.

Processing parts like the proteasome and TAP are near-identical in everyone. The model shows MHC diversity blocks global adaptation anyway. An escape that works in one person fails in the next. Diversity thus caps how far the virus can evolve ahead.
plos-pone-0003625:
Joann Mudge, Neil A. Miller, Irina Khrebtukova, and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It searches for the roots of schizophrenia, a serious mental illness that runs in families. The team used mRNA sequencing on brain tissue taken after death, focusing on the cerebellum.

By combining gene sequence data with other genetic evidence, the study found changed activity in genes for synaptic vesicle transport. Those vesicles are the tiny sacs that carry chemical messages between brain cells. The result points to faulty message handling as one part of how schizophrenia develops.
plos-pone-0003725:
Brian B. Gowen, Donald F. Smee, Min-Hui Wong, and colleagues published this drug study in PLOS ONE in 2008. A growing list of arenaviruses cause viral hemorrhagic fever, a severe illness with leaking blood vessels. Ribavirin is the only licensed drug for some of these infections, and it has limits.

The team tested the drug T-705 in an animal model, treating late stage disease. T-705 worked against the infection and showed reduced toxicity compared with ribavirin. The results suggest an alternative for infections that are usually treated only after they are already advanced.
plos-pone-0003825:
Tzvia Abramson, Hassya Kedem, and David A. Relman published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Bordetella pertussis is the bacterium behind whooping cough. One of its surface proteins, filamentous hemagglutinin, helps it attach to airway cells. The authors asked what that protein does to host immune signaling.

They report that filamentous hemagglutinin modulates the NF-kB pathway, a master switch of immune responses. Tuning that pathway can damp or redirect the host's defenses. The result shows one way the bacterium shapes its reception while it settles into the respiratory tract.
plos-pone-0003925:
Masashi Tachikawa modeled how changing conditions split species in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Living systems always face swings in their surroundings. Species evolve under those swings and often end up robust to them. Diversity in nature also grows through evolution under change.

The author asked how swings themselves shape that growth of diversity. His mathematical model of an ecosystem shows fluctuation driving evolutionary branching. In branching, one lineage splits into distinct forms over time. The model suggests changeable worlds may breed diversity faster than stable ones. It offers theory that field studies can test against real ecosystems.
plos-pone-0004025:
Abdullah Al Mahmud, Gabriele Amore, and Giorgio Bernardi studied genome makeup and gene control in sea urchins in 2008. Gene activity is usually credited to regulatory DNA regions alone. Those regions are built from modules of transcription factor binding sites. The authors questioned whether wider genome composition also matters.

Their PLOS ONE article reports compositional contexts affect gene control in embryos. The base makeup around a gene can sway its activity. That adds a background layer to the modular control picture. Sea urchin embryos give a clear system for testing such effects. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004125:
Carlos Driscoll and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks where the extinct Caspian tiger came from and how it relates to the living Amur tiger. The Caspian tiger once lived in river forests across Central Asia, in a range cut off from other tigers. Hunters drove it to extinction by 1970.

Because it vanished before modern genetic tests existed, its place among the tiger subspecies stayed unclear for over a century. The team read mitochondrial DNA, passed down through mothers, to place it on the tiger family tree. The study settles a long taxonomic puzzle using samples from a tiger no longer alive.
plos-pone-0004225:
Stefan Maas and Willemijn Gommans published this RNA study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells edit some RNA messages after they are written, changing single letters in the code. This A-to-I editing adds much of the variety in the mammalian transcriptome and can recode proteins, changing what they do.

The authors report a novel exon, a coding segment, in the mammalian ADAR2 gene, one of the genes for the editing enzymes themselves. The new segment extends the gene's open reading frame, the stretch that can be read as protein. Even the editors, it turns out, had an unread page in their own instructions.
plos-pone-0004325:
Chadi Touma and colleagues published this depression model study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, the stress hormone system, plays a key role in mood disorders such as major depression. Further hallmarks of depression include disturbed circadian rhythms in behaviour, hormones, and sleep.

The team studied mice selected for extremes in stress reactivity, bred to be high or low responders. They tracked behavioural, endocrine, and sleep changes resembling endophenotypes of major depression, traits that can be measured, which underlie the illness. Such mice offer a living model of the depressed body's daily rhythm gone wrong. The mice were bred to react strongly or weakly to stress.
plos-pone-0004425: In 2009, Koehncke, Telschow, and Werren told the parasite's rise and fall. The germ's life and death shaped host evolution strongly. The tiny rider drove its hosts' genes hard. The study lights up germ-host arms races well. The germs twist insect breeding.
plos-pone-0004525: In 2009, Wopereis, Rubingh, and van Erk found subtle metabolic shifts after sugar loads. Metabolic profiling of the oral glucose tolerance test response detected small changes. The blood profiles flagged pre-disease states. The method aids early diagnosis. The changes were quite subtle.
plos-pone-0004625: In 2009, Tursun, Cochella, and Carrera built a glowing toolkit for worms. A toolkit and robust pipeline generated fosmid reporter genes in C elegans. The fluorescent tags tracked gene expression. The tool aids developmental biology research. The new pipeline is robust.
plos-pone-0004725: In 2009, Jansen and a team found a skin protein tracking psoriasis anew here. β-defensin-2 protein served as a serum signal for psoriasis activity. The blood levels reached biological meaning indeed. The study informs dermatology research. The protein activities are antimicrobial indeed.
dospassos-manhattan-transfer-1925:
Harper published Manhattan Transfer in New York and London, listing it among Dos Passos's early books. The list sets it beside One Man's Initiation, Three Soldiers, and Streets of Night. Its author was already known as a bold voice in American fiction by 1925.

New York City itself becomes the true hero of the novel. Dozens of lives flicker past in fragments and headlines: clerks, actors, newcomers, and con men. Together they paint the huge city as a machine that lifts people up and grinds them down. Bold in form and rapid in pace, the book stands as the great modern novel of Manhattan life.
undset-the-mistress-of-husaby-kristin-la:
Kristin Lavransdatter returns as a wife and estate holder in The Mistress of Husaby, the middle book of Undset's trilogy, in Archer's 1925 English version. Her home is the great farm of Husaby. Marriage, once her fierce goal, now brings strain and sorrow.

Her husband proves weak where she needs strength, and her sons grow wild. Old sins from her youth still weigh on her mind and faith. Undset shows married life and motherhood with rare honesty for any age. The tale deepens from romance into tragedy as Kristin's pride and guilt pull against each other.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-25:
Death comes for Jogues in Volume 25, published by Thwaites in 1898. The book covers the years 1644 and 1645 across Iroquois and French lands. Mohawk men kill the peacemaker who had come to save them.

Fellow priests tell of his death with heartbreaking, plain simplicity. They count him a saint even as they write the sad news. Grief runs through the reports, yet the mission work goes on. Baptisms, burials, and brave journeys fill the months that follow. His blood, in their eyes, seals the mission he loved and served so well. Sorrow and pride fill the closing reports of this book.
journal-of-discourses-vol-25:
Volume Twenty-Five, from 1886, stands near the great turning point. The discourses breathe strain as the Saints await a change they cannot see. Within a few years, plural marriage will end by church decree.

Nothing here names that surrender, yet tension fills every long sermon. Leaders preach obedience while the law closes each road around them. A people waits for deliverance with no clear sign of its form. Readers who know 1890's Manifesto feel the ground shifting below. The hardest choice in Mormon history gathers force in these tense pages. When the change came, this volume helped readers grasp its cost.
treaty-of-rio-1825:
Portugal and Brazil signed the Treaty of Rio de Janeiro in 1825, formally settling Brazil's break from Portuguese rule. King John of Portugal accepted Brazil as an independent empire under his son, Dom Pedro. Brazil had declared its independence three years earlier, but Lisbon's legal recognition still had to be won at the negotiating table.

The text records Portugal's recognition, the titles each ruler would keep, and the financial terms that came with the settlement. Unlike the wars that freed Spanish America, this separation was closed by agreement between father and son. Brazil became a sovereign nation with its monarchy intact and its new status accepted in Europe.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol7-1925:
The seventh volume of Holdsworth's History of English Law appeared in 1925. Holdsworth's project, pursued at Oxford over decades, aimed to record the whole growth of English law. By the seventh volume the story had passed the age of revolution and entered calmer waters.

Volume 7 covers the eighteenth century, the age of Mansfield in the courts and Blackstone in the study. Holdsworth describes a law polished into system: commercial law modernized for a trading nation, and the great commentaries giving the whole a shape students could learn. It was the law's Augustan age, elegant and confident. Holdsworth treats it with the respect of a man who loved the tradition he chronicled. The volume remains a standard guide to the century that made the common law a world system.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol8-1925:
Holdsworth issued the eighth volume of his History of English Law in 1925. The history had grown from medieval beginnings through revolution and Augustan polish. Its author, by now the dean of English legal historians, turned to the century of reform.

Volume 8 covers the first half of the nineteenth century. Bentham's fierce attack on the old law opens the story, and the great reforms follow. Courts were rebuilt, procedures simplified, and whole fields of law cleaned of archaic clutter. Holdsworth tells of the law's modernization with the zeal of a historian who had lived to see its results. The old order is swept away in these pages, reform's triumph recorded act by act. The volume is essential reading on how Victorian England remade its law.
moore-defence-of-common-sense-1925:
George Edward Moore published A Defence of Common Sense in 1925, and it became his most famous short work. Moore, a Cambridge philosopher, wrote against skeptics who doubted the plain truths of everyday life. His method was disarmingly direct: state what we all know, and hold it more firmly than any theory that denies it.

The essay lists truisms Moore claims to know with certainty, such as that the earth existed long before his birth. In its best-known passage, tied to his lectures of the period, he proves an external world by holding up one hand, then another. The plain statement shook philosophy because it refused the skeptic's terms altogether. The piece is often called the shortest revolution in thought ever written, and it still anchors debates about knowledge.
cia-0000009125:
Huu Quan village, in Thuy Nguyen district, is pinpointed in a January 1972 report of an American prisoner sighted there. Thuy Nguyen lies near Haiphong, across the river from the port city. Village-level detail gave analysts a rare precise point on the prisoner map.

A named village could be checked against bombing records, local reports, and other sightings. The same village appears in an earlier 1967 report in these files, suggesting a place that kept surfacing. Comparing both entries shows how prisoner locations accumulated over years. This report adds the 1972 point to that small and telling geography.
cia-0000009825:
An American jet pilot was captured in Khammouane province in May 1965, a report filed in January 1967 states. Khammouane, in central Laos, carried the passes where supply routes crossed toward Vietnam. Jet pilots downed there fell far inside the secret war.

It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d225:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 August 1862, and the letter is printed as Document 225 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was acting for Lord Lyons at the British legation in Washington.

August opened with the war's center shifting back to northern Virginia, where a new campaign was gathering. Stuart's letters to Seward carried British requests and protests in the formal manner of the legation. Read with Seward's replies around it, this letter shows the two offices grinding through wartime business. They ground on even as armies moved within a few days' ride of the capital.
frus-1862-d325:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 12 September 1862 in a letter printed as Document 325 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Five days later the armies met at Antietam, but in Paris the talk was of mediation drafts and Mexican reinforcements. Dayton's job was to keep those two files separate in French minds, so Mexico would not buy the South a friend. His report from this week sits in the file just before the battle news broke the pattern. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d425:
Horace J. Perry sent this report from the Madrid legation to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 August 1862. It is Document 425 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Mid-August 1862 found the Madrid mission in transition, with Gustav Koerner arriving to take over as minister while Perry stayed on as secretary. Perry's reports bridged the change, keeping Washington informed about Spanish policy without a gap. Spain still held the keys to Cuba's ports, and its stance in Mexico was settling into watchful distance from France. A reader gets from letters like this the steady, factual feed on which Seward built his Spanish policy.
frus-1862-d525:
On 5 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 525 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

November brought the dismissal of McClellan and France's proposal for joint mediation in the war, which the Union refused. Seward's orders that month repeated the refusal to every post, great and small, The Hague included. Pike's Netherlands had no part in the mediation scheme, but a single line held everywhere was the policy's strength. The dispatch is part of the late-autumn file of that year. In it the Union, bloodied but standing, told Europe plainly that the war was an American question. It said the war would stay one.
frus-1862-d625:
On 1 April 1862, the day after his previous order, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a further instruction to Edward Joy Morris at Constantinople. It is Document 625 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Back-to-back orders to the farthest post in Europe suggest an enclosure or a second subject that could not travel in the same letter. The Ottoman file's business ran to the protection of American citizens and commerce in the Levant. There, consuls did the daily work. They did it under the minister's eye. Seward's paired instructions gave Morris the Department's mind on that business in full. Together the two letters show the care Washington took with a mission three months' post from home.
frus-1863p1-d25:
This second letter of 5 January 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams in London. It is document 25 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Paired letters like these are a mark of the exchange all through the volume.

Seward often split his orders so each sheet held one clear point. Adams, in turn, could act on each as its matter ripened in his talks with the British. This letter is the mate to document 24, written the same day. Together they open Washington's side of the London file for 1863, in the week the war took on a new cause.
frus-1863p1-d125:
Charles Francis Adams dated this dispatch 12 March 1863, though the printed volume sets it after letters of 19 March. Adams was the American minister in London, writing to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is document 125 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Stray dates are a quirk of these printed files, where late or loose sheets were set where they fit. The work in the letter is Adams's own: a report from the post that tracked Britain's mind on the war. Read on its true date, it fills a gap in mid-March. Read in its printed place, it is a small lesson in how the record was built.
frus-1863p1-d225:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 July 1863. It is document 225 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d325:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 24 November 1862. It appears as document 325 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d425:
Secretary of State William H. Seward received a letter dated 26 March 1863 from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d525:
Document 525, dated 22 May 1863, records a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d625:
From Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart to Secretary William H. Seward: a letter dated 29 September 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. Stuart was holding the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was away on leave, so the channel ran through him that season.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020225:
Livia de Hoz, Stephen J. Martin, and Richard G. M. Morris explored lost memories in rats for PLOS Biology in 2004. A rat that learns where things are can seem to forget over time. The team asked whether the memory is truly gone or just hard to reach.

A reminder cue brought the lost spatial memory back. That means forgetting was a failure of retrieval, not of storage, at least in this case. The result matters for how memory loss is understood. If traces persist but cannot be reached, then prompts and cues may restore more than expected. The study gives a neat animal model for telling stored memories apart from reachable ones.
plos-pone-0000125:
Neil J. Gemmell and Jon Slate published this short genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It addresses heterozygote advantage, the idea that carrying two different copies of a gene can beat carrying two matching copies. Here the trait under study is fecundity, how many offspring an organism produces.

Heterozygote advantage is one classic way that genetic variety stays in a population instead of being weeded out. The authors weigh the evidence for this effect on reproductive output. The question matters well beyond one species, because it helps explain why populations keep diversity that looks, at first glance, like it should disappear.
plos-pone-0000225:
Annika C. Karlsson, Astrid K. N. Iversen, Joan M. Chapman, and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2007. CTL responses are attacks by killer T cells on virus-infected cells. The authors track how these responses broaden, one target after another, in early HIV-1 infection. They link that broadening to viral escape, mutations that let the virus dodge attack.

Early immune responses shape the whole course of HIV infection. As each new T cell target appears, the virus mutates away from it, in a chase the authors document. Understanding that race informs vaccine design, which aims to aim the immune system at targets the virus cannot easily change.
plos-pone-0000325:
Xiang Jia Min and Donal A. Hickey published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. DNA barcodes are short, standard gene stretches used to identify species. The authors show that barcodes also provide a quick preview of a species' mitochondrial genome composition. One small piece summarizes features of the whole molecule.

A preview from a barcode saves the cost of sequencing whole mitochondrial genomes for every specimen. The authors test how much information the barcode region carries about the rest. The result adds value to the vast barcode libraries being built for species identification.
plos-pone-0000425:
Sol Efroni, Carl F. Schaefer, and Kenneth H. Buetow sorted cancers by the biological pathways active in them, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Two tumors can look alike under the microscope yet behave differently. Instead of cataloging single genes, the team analyzed pathway activity to identify the key processes underlying cancer phenotypes, the observable traits of each tumor.

Grouping cancers by the processes they depend on could reveal shared weaknesses that cut across tumor types. A drug aimed at a process, rather than at one gene, might then serve several groups at once. The approach reflects a shift in cancer research from lists of mutations toward maps of how cells are rewired.
plos-pone-0000525:
R. David Hawkins and colleagues profiled gene activity in healing ear tissue, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Some animals can regrow inner ear sensory tissue, the hair-cell-bearing epithelia whose loss causes deafness in humans. The team produced large scale gene expression profiles of regenerating inner ear sensory epithelia.

A profile taken during regrowth lists the genes the tissue switches on to rebuild itself. Comparing that list with the mammalian ear, which does not regenerate, highlights what is missing. Deafness research uses such profiles as a parts list for attempts to wake the same program in human ears.
plos-pone-0000625:
Farooq Kiani, Sonja Schwarzl, Stefan Fischer and colleagues built three-dimensional models of a faulty enzyme, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. The enzyme is G6PD, and losing its function is the most common inborn error of metabolism in the world. The authors cite an estimate of 400 million people affected. In Germany, though, the condition is very rare.

Working from known G6PD crystal structures, the team modeled variants found in people of German ancestry. A 3D model shows how a changed enzyme part might break its working shape. Such models help explain why some variants cause severe disease while others stay mild.
plos-pone-0000725:
Odile Launay, Christine Durier, Corinne Desaint and colleagues compared two routes for delivering an HIV vaccine in the ANRS VAC16 trial. Their 2007 PLOS ONE objective was safety and cellular immune response. Healthy, HIV-uninfected volunteers received a candidate vaccine called LIPO-4, built from HIV lipopeptides. One group got it intradermally, into the skin; the other intramuscularly, into muscle.

The trial was randomized and open-label, run in France at six sites with 24 weeks of follow-up. Intradermal delivery is dose-sparing, stretching limited vaccine further. If skin delivery with less vaccine matches muscle delivery, vaccination campaigns gain reach. Cellular responses, T cell reactions, were the measure that mattered here.
plos-pone-0000825:
Ann-Charlotte Lundstedt, Shane McCarthy, Mattias C.U. Gustafsson and colleagues proposed a genetic reason some people suffer the worst urinary infections. For unknown reasons, urinary tract infections cluster in certain individuals. Their 2007 PLOS ONE paper proposes a new, gene-based cause of susceptibility to acute pyelonephritis. That is the most severe form of UTI, the kind that reaches the kidneys. The IL-8 receptor, CXCR1, was identified as a candidate.

A receptor for IL-8 helps summon white blood cells to fight bacteria in the urinary tract. If inherited variants blunt that summons, kidneys may be left undefended. A genetic basis would explain family clustering, and could flag patients who need aggressive prevention.
plos-pone-0000925:
Richard Ortega, Peter Cloetens, Guillaume Deves and colleagues pictured iron stored inside dopamine vesicles at nano scale, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Disturbed metal balance in the brain is suspected in nerve cell death. Until now, no tool could map metals inside neurons finely enough to test that idea.

The team developed a chemical nano-imaging setup for the job. With it, they could see iron held within the tiny vesicles that store dopamine, a key brain signal chemical. A clear picture of where iron sits in healthy cells sets the baseline. Later work can then ask what changes when neurons begin to fail.
plos-pone-0001025:
Qi Wang and Yuan-Ping Pang offered a safer way to relax small molecules into their bound shapes on a computer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. When a drug molecule settles into a protein pocket, it takes a bound conformation, a specific folded shape. Computer minimization finds such shapes by lowering the molecule's energy.

The catch: a shallow energy dip may not stop the process, and the molecule folds wrongly. Their procedure watches the minimization with normal mode analysis, a check on the molecule's vibration patterns. A monitored stop should give shapes that match how molecules really sit in pockets. Drug modelers need exactly that reliability.
plos-pone-0001125:
Stress during development can leave lasting marks on the brain. Xia Wang, David Green, Stephen Roberts, and co-authors tested one form of stress, heat, in the fruit fly Drosophila, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on the mushroom body, a brain region flies use for smell-based learning.

The study asks whether thermal stress disrupts how the mushroom body develops and how well adult flies learn odors. Earlier work had shown that many kinds of stress disturb brain development in every model system tried. This paper ties a specific stress to a specific brain structure and a measurable behavior, smell learning.
plos-pone-0001225:
Some blood cancers hide chromosome damage that standard tests cannot see. Lukasz Gondek and colleagues applied SNP arrays to patients with atypical myeloproliferative and myelodysplastic syndromes. Their study appeared in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. SNP arrays are chips that read hundreds of thousands of single-letter DNA variants.

The authors show that SNP array karyotyping detects uniparental disomy. In that condition, both copies of a chromosome segment come from one parent. It also detects cryptic chromosomal abnormalities that older methods miss. They studied patients with and without the JAK2 V617F mutation, a common driver in these diseases. Finer karyotyping can change diagnosis and treatment choices.
plos-pone-0001325:
Certain short peptides can assemble themselves into coatings and scaffolds, making them attractive nano-biomaterials. Hong Yang, Shan-Yu Fung, and Mark Pritzker studied one model peptide, EAK16-II, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Ionic-complementary peptides carry alternating positive and negative charges that drive their assembly.

The authors present evidence that the peptide can assemble on and coat both hydrophilic and hydrophobic surfaces, water-loving and water-hating alike. Such coatings could engineer biosurfaces for implants, sensors, and cell culture. A single peptide that coats both surface types is a versatile tool. The peptide assembles on its own once applied.
plos-pone-0001425:
Enrique Caviedes-Vidal and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how bats take up food from the gut. Bats tend to have less gut tissue than like sized mammals that do not fly. A small gut saves weight, which helps flight. The team asked how bats still get enough food from that small gut.

They show that bats let a large share of food pass between gut cells, not just through them. That route breaks the usual mammal pattern. It lets a small gut act like a much larger one. The finding recasts how flight shaped the bat body, gut included, over time.
plos-pone-0001525:
Joshua Herbeck and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on whether HIV is growing more or less harsh. Past cohort data and lab tests had given clashing answers, with claims of falling, flat, and rising harm. The team tested the change claim in North American data. They used set marks of virus strength over time.

They found a lack of proof for a shift in HIV strength in this region. A flat verdict from sound data still counts. It means care and spread plans need not chase a moving target on this front. It also shows how weak methods can breed false trends.
plos-pone-0001625:
Cédric Patthey, Lena Gunhaga, and Thomas Edlund studied how the brain, spinal cord, and sense organs begin to form in the early embryo. Their 2008 PLOS ONE research article focuses on two signal families, Wnt and BMP, that cells use to tell nearby cells what to become. The central nervous system grows from the neural plate, while the peripheral system grows from cells at its border.

For the senses to work, these two systems must grow in step, so that circuits form in the right places. The authors trace how Wnt and BMP signals coordinate the growth of neural plate, neural crest, and placodal cells. The full text gives the embryo experiments and the signals they recorded. The work helps explain how a flat sheet of early cells turns into a wired nervous system.
plos-pone-0001725:
Gregory P. Bisson, Tendani Gaolathe, Robert Gross, and their co-authors warned that HIV treatment success may be overstated, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tracking how well global antiretroviral therapy scale-up works is a health priority. In resource-limited settings, though, many patients are lost to follow-up after starting treatment, and their true outcomes are unknown.

If many of those lost patients have died, published survival figures will look too good. The authors examined definitive outcomes of lost patients and what they imply for reported survival after HAART. The full text gives the tracing results and the corrected survival estimates. Honest numbers decide whether scale-up is truly working or needs fixing.
plos-pone-0001825:
Daniel A. Beard, Kalyan C. Vinnakota, and Fan Wu worked out detailed enzyme kinetics for a core metabolic enzyme in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Citrate synthase runs the first step of the citric acid cycle, the cell's central energy pathway. The paper analyzes the compulsory-ordered ternary mechanism used by two-substrate, two-product enzymes.

Their treatment accounts for inhibitors binding to each of the four enzyme states and keeps the kinetic constants consistent with the reaction equilibrium constant. The full text gives the derivations and the worked example. Rigorous kinetics of this kind, called biochemical species kinetics, improves computer models of metabolism used in drug and biofuel research.
plos-pone-0001925:
Mathias Gehrmann and co-authors asked why tumor cells, but not healthy cells, show a stress protein on their surface, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, Hsp70, is the main stress-induced member of its family. When it sits on a tumor's outer membrane, it flags a worse or better outlook in some cancers, such as leukemia.

The team traced the display to a fat-like molecule in the membrane called Gb3. As the title states, Gb3 enables the tumor-specific placement of Hsp70 on the surface. That detail matters because surface Hsp70 can draw immune attack. A drug that shifts Gb3 might make more tumors show the flag.
plos-pone-0002025:
Lina Dahl and co-authors studied a gene that keeps young blood cells dividing, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. How the blood system expands in the fetal liver, stem cells and all, is largely unknown. The gene Lhx2 was a candidate driver, since it is active in that setting.

The team grew embryonic stem cells into embryoid bodies, small balls that mimic early development, and switched Lhx2 on. As the title states, its expression promoted self-renewal of a distinct early blood progenitor cell. A gene that keeps blood precursors young could help labs grow blood stem cells for therapy.
plos-pone-0002125:
Phuoc Tran and co-authors asked what happens when two cancer genes are switched off at once. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Lab models had shown that tumors need a cancer gene to stay switched on, a trait called oncogene addiction. Most real cancers, though, are driven by several gene changes at once, which makes it hard to tell which ones the tumor truly needs.

Working with lung adenocarcinomas and lymphomas in mice, the team turned off both MYC and K-Ras together. Doing so reversed tumor growth in their models. The finding supports the idea that hitting more than one driver gene at once could be a stronger way to treat cancer.
plos-pone-0002225:
Allan Reiss and co-authors scanned the brains of people whose laughter can knock out their muscles. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cataplexy affects some people with narcolepsy, roughly 1 in 2,000 people overall. Strong feelings, above all laughter, can trigger a brief loss of muscle tone that leaves a person limp but awake.

The study aimed to find how the hypothalamus, a small brain region tied to sleep and emotion, responds to humor in these patients. Its responses looked anomalous next to those of healthy subjects. The work helps explain how an emotion can flip a switch in the brain and cut the body's strength.
plos-pone-0002325:
Wei Zhang, Song Liu, and Yaoqi Zhou presented an improved program for recognizing a protein's fold, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Predicting which known shape a new protein sequence will fold into is a central challenge in protein science. The team had built a series of methods, called SPARKS and SP2 through SP4, that score how well a sequence fits a known structure.

Their new method, SP5, adds torsion angle profiles, the twist patterns along the protein backbone, and a smarter penalty for gaps. Better fold recognition means more proteins of unknown shape can be assigned a likely structure from sequence alone, guiding experiments that follow.
plos-pone-0002425:
Faça and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Vitor M. Faça, Aviva P. Ventura, Mathew P. Fitzgibbon, among others. Its subject is proteomic Analysis of Ovarian Cancer Cells Reveals Dynamic Processes of Protein Secretion and Shedding of Extra-Cellular Domains. Elucidation of the repertoire of secreted and cell surface proteins of tumor cells is relevant to molecular diagnostics, tumor imaging and targeted therapies.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002525:
Takata and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Norio Takata, Hajime Hirase, among others. Its subject is cortical Layer 1 and Layer 2/3 Astrocytes Exhibit Distinct Calcium Dynamics In Vivo. Cumulative evidence supports bidirectional interactions between astrocytes and neurons, suggesting glial involvement of neuronal information processing in the brain.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002625:
Jürgen Konczak and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of haptic perception of object curvature in parkinson's disease. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Jürgen Konczak, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The haptic perception of the curvature of an object is essential for adequate object manipulation and critical for our guidance of actions. A further point appears in the abstract. This study investigated how the ability to perceive the curvature of an object is altered by Parkinson's disease (PD). Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002725:
In 2008, Karlijn I. van Aerde and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about prelimbic and infralimbic prefrontal cortex interact during fast network oscillations. The catalog record names Karlijn I. van Aerde first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The medial prefrontal cortex has been implicated in a variety of cognitive and executive processes such as decision making and working memory. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002825:
In 2008, Jerome J. Weis and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was effects of algal diversity on the production of biomass in homogeneous and heterogeneous nutrient environments: a microcosm experiment. Authorship is credited in the record to Jerome J. Weis and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. One of the most common questions addressed by ecologists over the past decade has been-how does species richness impact the production of community biomass?. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002925:
Thomas Fanshawe, Andrew Lynch, Ian Ellis and colleagues tackled a statistics problem in breast cancer grading in 2008. Pathologists grade tumor samples to guide care, yet past studies found only moderate agreement between raters. Missing ratings and many raters make judging that agreement harder still.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team sets out a way to assess agreement when rating data are incomplete. They apply it to a large but partial dataset of breast tumor grading. Better agreement measures help hospitals know how much weight a grade deserves and where training or review is needed most.
plos-pone-0003025:
Eliana Marengo, Luciana de Moraes, Marcella Faria and co-authors gave a leprosy heat shock protein to lupus-prone mice in 2008. Heat shock proteins guide protein assembly and transport and are highly conserved across life. The Hsp60 family is expressed at high levels and interacts with the immune system.

The treatment used Hsp65 from Mycobacterium leprae, the leprosy bacterium. It interfered with the progression of murine lupus, an autoimmune disease, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, a bacterial protein calming autoimmunity is counterintuitive but fits the idea that immune tuning can treat immune excess.
plos-pone-0003125:
Jean-Michel Benoist, Ivanne Pincedé, Kay Ballantyne and colleagues address a basic problem in pain research in this 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many tests of pain response in rats use reaction time, the gap between the start of a stimulus such as heat and the animal's response. Yet skin cannot be heated at once by normal means, which makes that timing hard to read.

The authors work out what parts of the reaction come from the body surface and what parts come from the central nervous system. Readers get a careful approach to psychophysics in the rat. It helps others judge what a simple reaction time can and cannot prove.
plos-pone-0003225:
Ting-Hua Huang, Meng-Jin Zhu, Xin-Yun Li and colleagues catalogue pig microRNAs in muscle in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs play critical roles in many important biological processes such as growth and development in mammals. In this study, the team identified hundreds of porcine microRNA candidates through computer prediction and analysed their expression in developing skeletal muscle using further methods.

Readers get both a discovery list and a developmental profile for pig muscle. Pigs are a major farm animal and a medical model, so their microRNA map has dual value. Muscle microRNAs may also guide breeding for meat traits.
plos-pone-0003325:
Alexander O. Vargas, Tiana Kohlsdorf, John F. Fallon and colleagues study digit identity in the bird wing in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Comparative morphology identifies the digits of the wing of birds as one, two and three, but they develop at embryological positions that become digits two, three and four in other amniotes. A hypothesis to explain this is that a homeotic frame shift of digital identity occurred in bird evolution.

The authors examine evolution of HoxD-11 expression in the bird wing, with insights from Alligator mississippiensis. Readers see gene expression used to test a classic anatomy puzzle. Alligators, as bird relatives, provide the comparison that makes the test possible.
plos-pone-0007425: Dengue infects millions yearly, and vaccine makers fear a vaccine could backfire by boosting a later, worse infection. To design a safer vaccine, the researchers mapped the exact spots on the dengue virus's outer shell that human antibodies latch onto. Knowing which patches the immune system sees is the first step toward a vaccine that protects without the dangerous side effects.
plos-pone-0007525: In asthma and allergies, a group of immune cells called Th2 cells drive airway inflammation. This study shows that a switch on those cells, the inducible costimulator ICOS, controls how many Th2 cells gather — and therefore how severe the inflammation gets. Because ICOS can be drugged, it is a promising target for calming overactive airways.
plos-pone-0007625: Work stress harms people — and this study suggests it harms horses too. Comparing horses with different workloads and conditions, the researchers found links between work routines and behavioral disorders like stereotypies. The finding treats the working horse as a fellow laborer whose job can damage its mind.
plos-pone-0007725: Cuckoo chicks hatch blind and naked, yet push host eggs from the nest. This study found the eviction effort carries a cost the chicks can recover from — a price of their murderous start. Even parasites pay for their virulence.
plos-pone-0007825: HIV's integrase was thought to act late, inserting viral DNA — but this study shows it boosts reverse transcription early, by binding the host factor SIP1/Gemin2. The interaction proved critical for infection. Integrase emerges as a multitasker, and a richer drug target.
plos-pone-0007925: HIV-positive women want clear answers about having babies. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Loutfy and colleagues surveyed fertility desires and intentions among HIV-positive women of reproductive age in Ontario. Longer lives and low mother-to-child transmission have made pregnancy a real option. The cross-sectional data help health services plan counseling and care for these mothers-to-be.
plos-pone-0008025: Huntington's disease clumps huntingtin protein in the brain — but this study found the inclusions throughout the body in a knock-in mouse model. The wide distribution shows Huntington's is a whole-body disease, not just a brain one.
plos-pone-0008125: A standard recipe for running reaction models on a computer got much faster. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Indurkhya and Beal sped up the Gillespie algorithm, a classic tool that plays out reactions step by step. The old version crawls on big networks because each step scans the whole set. By grouping like reactions and touching only what changed, the team cut the work sharply. The speedup brings whole-cell models within reach of normal machines.
plos-pone-0008225: Smoking was caught blocking the lung's antioxidant shield. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Garbin's team showed cigarette smoke silences the Nrf2/ARE defense pathway in young heavy smokers' blood cells. The pathway normally counters oxidative stress; its shutdown favors inflammation and artery damage. The blockade helps explain smoking's toll on vessels. The finding spotlights a pathway that quitting might restore.
